sources.text: The Taj Mahal was commissioned by the fifth Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as the mausoleum of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is a funerary complex rather than a palace: the tomb stands at the head of a walled garden, with a mosque to its west and a matching guest house, the jawab, to its east.
sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal (ref. 252); Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record

sources.text: Mumtaz Mahal died on 17 June 1631 at Burhanpur, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, while giving birth to her fourteenth child. She was buried first in a garden on the bank of the Tapti, and her body was brought to Agra in December 1631.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record

sources.text: Work began in 1632. The mausoleum itself was finished within about a decade, and the whole complex — the mosque, the guest house, the great gateway, the outer courtyard and the cloisters — was completed in 1653. Sources differ over exactly when the tomb building alone was considered done.
sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal (ref. 252)

sources.text: The chief architect named in the sources is Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, Shah Jahan's court architect, who worked with a board of architects including Mir Abd-ul Karim. The attribution rests on a verse by his son, Lutfullah Muhandis, rather than on a building record.
sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal (ref. 252); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Taj Mahal

sources.text: The mausoleum is a square of roughly 58.6 metres a side, raised on a marble plinth about 95 metres square and some 7 metres high. The walled complex covers about 17 hectares, with a charbagh garden roughly 300 metres square.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal (ref. 252)

sources.text: The main dome is a double shell. The outer bulbous dome is about 17.7 metres in diameter and rises roughly 35 metres above the roof on a cylindrical drum; the inner dome, seen from the chamber below, is about 24.4 metres high. Four smaller domed chhatris stand around it, and a gilded finial crowns the whole.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record

sources.text: Four minarets stand at the corners of the plinth, each about 40 metres high, and each leans very slightly outward from the tomb. The often-repeated explanation that they were tilted so as to fall away from the tomb in an earthquake is a guidebook tradition and is not documented in Mughal sources.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record

sources.text: The facing is white marble quarried at Makrana in Rajasthan, over 300 kilometres away; the gateway, mosque and jawab are of red sandstone from near Fatehpur Sikri. The inlay work, parchin kari, uses stones brought from far off — jasper from Punjab, turquoise from Tibet, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, sapphire from Sri Lanka, jade and crystal from China, carnelian from Arabia.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal (ref. 252)

sources.text: The inscriptions are Quranic verses in thuluth script by the Persian calligrapher Abd al-Haqq, whom Shah Jahan titled Amanat Khan; he signed his work within the marble, one of very few named craftsmen. The great gateway carries the lines: O soul, thou art at rest. Return to the Lord at peace with Him, and He at peace with you.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal site record; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Amanat Khan Shirazi

sources.text: Two famous stories about the Taj are legends, not history. The 'Black Taj' said to have been planned across the river rests solely on the account of the traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, and excavation at Mehtab Bagh in 1993 found a Mughal garden but no black marble. The story that Shah Jahan had the workers' hands cut off has no basis in any contemporary source.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Mehtab Bagh excavation record; historians S. Irfan Habib and Najaf Haider, cited in published fact-checks

sources.text: In the eighteenth century the Taj was stripped of its silver doors, chandeliers and carpets, which were melted down and never replaced. Viceroy Lord Curzon ordered a major restoration, completed in 1908, and presented a bronze lamp made in Cairo by Todros Badir, hung in the tomb chamber on 16 February 1908.
sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Taj Mahal conservation record

sources.text: In 1942 the dome was hidden under bamboo scaffolding to look like a stockpile of stores, in case of air attack, and during later wars the marble was covered with green-dyed tarpaulins. The Taj Mahal was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983 under cultural criterion (i), is a centrally protected monument in the care of the Archaeological Survey of India, and is shielded by the Taj Trapezium Zone created by the Supreme Court of India in December 1996.
sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal (ref. 252); Archaeological Survey of India; Supreme Court of India, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, 30 December 1996

intro.en-IN: I am the Taj Mahal. Shah Jahan raised me for Mumtaz Mahal — come closer, and I will tell you about her.
intro.hi-IN: मैं ताज महल हूँ। शाहजहाँ ने मुझे मुमताज़ महल के लिए बनवाया था — पास आओ, मैं तुम्हें उनकी कहानी सुनाऊँ।
intro.ur-IN: میں تاج محل ہوں۔ شاہجہاں نے مجھے ممتاز محل کے لیے بنوایا تھا — قریب آؤ، میں تمہیں ان کی کہانی سناؤں۔
intro.bn-IN: আমি তাজমহল। শাহজাহান আমাকে মমতাজ মহলের জন্য গড়েছিলেন — কাছে এসো, আমি তাঁর কথা বলি।
intro.ta-IN: நான் தாஜ் மகால். ஷாஜகான் என்னை மும்தாஜ் மகாலுக்காக எழுப்பினார் — அருகில் வாருங்கள், அவரைப் பற்றிச் சொல்கிறேன்.
intro.te-IN: నేను తాజ్ మహల్. షాజహాన్ నన్ను ముంతాజ్ మహల్ కోసం కట్టించాడు — దగ్గరకు రండి, ఆమె గురించి చెబుతాను.
intro.mr-IN: मी ताजमहाल. शहाजहानने मला मुमताज महलसाठी उभारले — जवळ या, मी तिची गोष्ट सांगतो.
intro.kn-IN: ನಾನು ತಾಜ್ ಮಹಲ್. ಷಹಜಹಾನ್ ನನ್ನನ್ನು ಮುಮ್ತಾಜ್ ಮಹಲ್‌ಗಾಗಿ ಕಟ್ಟಿಸಿದ — ಹತ್ತಿರ ಬನ್ನಿ, ಅವಳ ಕಥೆ ಹೇಳುತ್ತೇನೆ.
